summary: Describes a standard method for storing Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) keys and signatures in the DNS, using the KEY and SIG resource record types. It was later updated by RFC 6944.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2536 defines how DNS stores DSA public keys and signatures in KEY and SIG records. It specifies the field order and size, while relying on other documents for the overall DNS security record format.

subtitle: The field layouts for DSA public keys and signatures in DNS KEY and SIG records.

tldr.problem: DNS security defines records for keys and signatures, but needed a standard layout for Digital Signature Algorithm data.
tldr.mechanism: A DSA public key uses algorithm number 3 in a KEY record, with fields T, Q, P, G, and Y. A SIG record carries T, R, and S for the signature.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2536 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 6944. It notes a 1024-bit maximum key size under the DSA standard it references and the need for good random numbers.

today: RFC 2536 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1999 and was updated by RFC 6944. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: DSA Data in DNS
sections.content:
DNS security adds digital signatures and cryptographic keys to DNS records. RFC 2536 specifies how to represent keys and signatures made with the U.S. Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA).

The RFC assumes familiarity with DSA and states that DSA implementation is mandatory for the DNS security system it describes. The surrounding KEY and SIG record structure is defined in RFC 2535.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines the DSA-specific data stored in DNS records. The general DNS security record format comes from another RFC.

sections.title: Fields in a DSA KEY Record
sections.content:
A DSA public key is stored in a KEY resource record using algorithm number 3. Its algorithm-specific data contains a one-octet T, a 20-octet Q, and P, G, and Y, each 64 + 8*T octets long.

The parameter T ranges from 0 through 8. The private value X is used to calculate the public value Y but is not placed in the public key record. Values are stored in big-endian network order.

The KEY record does not carry its validity period. A SIG record that authenticates the KEY records supplies that information.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key is stored as a fixed sequence of numbers. The one-octet T value sets the lengths of P, G, and Y; the private key is not included.

sections.title: Fields in a DSA SIG Record
sections.content:
The DSA signature portion of a SIG record contains T, R, and S, in that order. T is one octet, while R and S are each 20 octets.

The signer hashes the data with SHA-1, chooses a random K in the range defined by the RFC, and computes R and S using the DSA procedure. T is copied from the public key; the RFC retains it as a possible extension point.
sections.plainLanguage: A DSA signature is represented by two 20-octet values, R and S, preceded by the key-size parameter T. The SIG record's other fields are defined by RFC 2535.

sections.title: Performance and Record Size
sections.content:
The RFC says DSA and RSA have roughly similar signature-generation speed. With sufficient precomputation, DSA signing and key generation can be faster, while verification can be an order of magnitude slower than RSA with a small public exponent.

DNS implementations of the period were optimized for transfers typically below 512 bytes including overhead. The RFC recommends keeping KEY record sets as small as adequate security permits, remembering that a secure zone also returns an authenticating SIG record.
sections.plainLanguage: DSA can make signatures quickly, but checking them can take longer than checking RSA signatures in the comparison described here. Larger DNS record sets also increase the size of responses.

sections.title: Key Trust and Randomness
sections.content:
A key retrieved from DNS should not be trusted unless it was securely obtained or independently verified according to the user's security policy. The appropriate key strength depends on local policy.

The DSA standard referenced by this RFC limits key size to 1024 bits. DSA also requires frequent high-quality random numbers; manipulated values can expose the private key, so trusted random-number generation is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS key needs secure verification before an application trusts it. DSA also depends on unpredictable random numbers; poor random values can expose the private key.

sections.title: Future Values of T
sections.content: Giving a meaning to a T value not defined by this document requires an IETF standards action. The unallocated values are intended for possible future extensions to the Digital Signature Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC leaves some T values undefined for later extensions. A standards action is required before an undefined value can gain a meaning.
